stories.headline: Meta launches Muse Wonder, claiming a lead over Opus 5.5 on long coding
stories.standfirst: Meta says Muse Wonder Full scores 57.5% on SWE-Marathon against 46.3% for Claude Opus 5.5, and Artificial Analysis ranks it second overall, two points behind.
body: Meta released two models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, which it calls its most capable yet and built for "personal and professional agentic tasks", according to its research blog. Mark Zuckerberg wrote that it has been just over a year since Meta Superintelligence Labs began, and that Muse Wonder "brings us to the frontier". TechCrunch calls it Meta's first attempt at a frontier model.

Muse Wonder is available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, Meta's coding product. Muse Wonder Full, the higher-effort version, is available only to Muse Code subscribers and is not served through the API, TechCrunch reports. Meta says Muse Wonder will soon power its Muse agent, starting with subscribers. TechCrunch gives the API price as $4.00 per million input tokens and $20.00 per million output tokens.

The headline numbers are Meta's own. Rohan Paul, an AI commentator, relayed Meta's chart: on SWE-Marathon, an ultra-long engineering test, Full scores 57.5 against 46.3 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 42.5 for GPT-6 Astra. On DeepSWE 1.1 it scores 79.0 against 74.2 for Opus 5.5, which Meta says came from independent third-party runs. Meta also names Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark and a memory test, but its blog text gives no scores.

The one outside measurement so far is Artificial Analysis, which says Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full score 52 and 56 on its Intelligence Index v4.3 at maximum reasoning effort, up from 48 for Muse Spark 1.3, released six weeks earlier. The firm says Full ranks in the top three on six of ten component evaluations, first on CritPt and GDP.pdf with narrow leads, and lifts Terminal-Bench 4.0 from 33% to 57%. Commentators put Full two points behind Opus 5.5 overall.

Meta pitches two features for agents. Active Memory keeps user context across conversations and retrieves it when relevant; Active Focus keeps a model working through blockers and asks for clarification before important actions, the blog says. Meta says the models have its strongest safeguards yet against chemical, biological, nuclear and cyber misuse, and that a full safety report will follow. The page gives no context length.

Treat the comparisons with caution. The benchmark and "state-of-the-art" claims come from Meta, TechCrunch has not verified them, and the Artificial Analysis result covers only part of the picture: commentators noted that Opus still leads on ProgramBench and on the overall index. Hands-on tests from people outside Meta have only just started to appear.

stories.headline: Meta's Wang admits Muse Wonder was not trained on 3D demo games
stories.standfirst: Meta's Alexandr Wang says the team did not explicitly train Muse Wonder on 3D demo games, after users posted weak Minecraft clones, while developer Theo ranks it level with Opus 5.5.
body: Hours after Meta released Muse Wonder, users began posting 3D game demos that fell short of rival models. Alexandr Wang of Meta answered on X. "Whole team feels dumb now, but it's true," he wrote. "We did not explicitly train our model on 3d demo games." He added that Meta should "obviously in retrospect" have done some, and asked people to try the model on real coding.

Wang also conceded limits. Replying to one user, he said Wonder is not as good as Opus 5.5 on coding, "for sure". He said bugs were being looked into. Another user posted a failed "make a minecraft clone" result. Wang said his own run of that prompt gave a much better answer. He suspects a bug.

Defence came from outside Meta. Theo, who builds the T3 Code agent tool and says he added Muse support there last week, argued that people are discounting Wonder over 3D demos. In his words: "3d game demos are cool! They don't represent real code work at all." That post had 773 likes when the feed was read at about 20:00 UTC on Monday.

Theo's own ranking, at 1,220 likes in the same read, puts Opus 5.5 and Muse Wonder in S tier and GPT-6.1 Sol in A tier. He says he mostly pairs Opus with Wonder, using Wonder for code review and architecture review, and calls it cheaper than Fable and Opus for similar quality. These are one developer's opinions, not a benchmark.

Cost may be the harder question. The Decoder reports that Artificial Analysis measures Muse Wonder at $4.52 per task on its index, against $1.60 for Muse Spark 1.3 and $5.98 for Claude Opus 5.5. Meta lists Wonder at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output. No price has been published for Muse Wonder Full, and the detailed system card has not yet appeared.

stories.headline: Sakana AI says a 27B model got better by training on its own team
stories.standfirst: Sakana AI says two rounds of a 27B open model organising copies of itself into a team, then training on the best runs, lifted research scores per output token 1.2 to 1.6 times.
body: Sakana AI published a paper on Sunday describing Multi-Agent Self-Supervision, or MASS, a method in which a single model plays solver, workflow optimiser and judge. According to the company's blog post, the aim is to keep improving a model on open-ended research tasks that humans may struggle to grade. The code is listed as released on GitHub.

The loop has two parts, per the paper. In the first, the model evolves multi-agent workflows, deciding how subagents talk to each other, and picks a winner. In the second, the champion workflow runs 18 times per task, the model ranks the outputs, and the best runs are used to fine-tune it with LoRA, so the coordination is baked into the weights.

Sakana says it ran two rounds starting from Qwen3.6-27B, on 12 synthetic research tasks across finance, robotics and pharmacy, three of them held out for testing. Judged by GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, which never fed back into training, the tuned model won 69.9 percent of held-out comparisons against the base model after round two, the authors report.

Score per output token against the base model reached 1.60 times on MLR-Bench, 1.35 on DSBench, 1.28 on AstaBench E2E-Hard and 1.20 on ScienceAgentBench, according to the paper. Coding did not improve: Terminal-Bench 2.0 came in at 0.96 times and SWE-bench Verified at 0.94. The authors also report that the model's agreement with the outside judges rose from 73 to 93 percent.

The authors list their own caveats. The test suite is small, and team runs generate about 2.4 times as many tokens, which the per-token figures do not charge for data generation or search. They warn that shared blind spots could let flawed results reinforce themselves. No independent group has reproduced the results, and everything above is Sakana's own account.

stories.headline: Subquadratic launches SubQ Snap, claiming 100,000 tokens read in a second
stories.standfirst: Subquadratic says SubQ Snap handles 384,000 tokens of context, costs $0.05 per million input tokens and beats its own Jev model on 13 of 16 enterprise tests.
body: Subquadratic launched SubQ Snap on Monday, which the San Francisco company calls a multimodal "decision model" for fast, long-context choices inside agent workflows. A decision model reads supplied context against a defined question and returns a structured answer, such as a choice, score or label, instead of open-ended text, according to the company's page. It is a separate product from SubQ, the long-context language model it announced earlier this year.

Subquadratic says Snap takes up to 384,000 tokens of context, against the 32,000 it says current decision models see. The company says it can process 100,000 tokens and return a decision in about one second, though its page gives no latency table. It suggests uses such as curating context for coding agents, recommendation systems and support-queue triage. The company credits its Subquadratic Sparse Attention method for the efficiency.

Pricing is listed at $0.05 per million input tokens, with output free, and the company offers 100 million free tokens to the first 10,000 users. Access runs through console.subq.ai, with enterprise requests handled by sales. Reports of the launch describe access as limited.

The benchmarks are the company's own, and compare Snap with Jev, a model the page never explains. Subquadratic says Snap scores 61.7 on its Decision Index against 57.9 for Jev, 74.0 against 48.0 on a multi-document test, and leads on 13 of 16 enterprise benchmarks, averaging 67.5 to 61.6. It says Snap trails on three, by 7.6 points on When2Call.

No independent results have been published for Snap. The page cites no outside evaluator for it, and the "multimodal" claim does not say which modalities are supported. Subquadratic's earlier 12-million-token SubQ drew scepticism from commentators who said its numbers were not reproducible, and one report says its chief technology officer confirmed that model builds on someone else's open-source weights.

stories.headline: Nvidia opens Vera Rubin rack designs to the Open Compute Project
stories.standfirst: Nvidia says its Vera Rubin rack and compute-tray designs are now open through the OCP, with racks of up to 250kW and a Cisco-backed optics standard.
body: Nvidia said on Monday at the Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose that it has contributed Vera Rubin rack and compute-tray designs to the project through its MGX architecture. The company's blog post says MGX 1.2 adds blind-mate liquid cooling, a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar and native 19-inch equipment support.

By Nvidia's account, MGX 1.2 supports racks of up to 250kW, with fanless liquid-cooled compute trays. The company also described a Vera CPU rack for agentic AI work such as tool calling and orchestration. It said Vera Rubin NVL72 remains its base for large-scale training and inference.

On networking, Nvidia said Meta is adopting its Spectrum-6 switches, rated at 102.4Tb/s. The design could link more than 100,000 GPUs across up to eight network planes, Nvidia said. Omar Baldonado, a senior director at Meta, is quoted saying the two companies are working to make multiplane fabrics operationally scalable. No independent measurements have been published.

Cisco and Nvidia also announced USFP, a pluggable optics form factor that targets 400Gb/s per lane. Nvidia says that is about 1.3 times more power-efficient and four times denser than 200Gb/s-per-lane optics. TE Connectivity and Amphenol will supply the connectors. Tom's Hardware reported that AMD showed a Helion rack design with up to 32,768 Zen 6 cores, shipping next year.

stories.headline: Katzenberg and ex-Sora lead said to be seeking access to Sora
stories.standfirst: The Information reports a filmmaker-focused startup is negotiating deep access to OpenAI's shuttered Sora video model, which it could customise and sell, with OpenAI taking equity.
body: A stealthy startup co-founded by the Hollywood executive Jeffrey Katzenberg and Sora's former research lead Bill Peebles is in talks with OpenAI over deep access to the video model, according to The Information. Reporter Stephanie Palazzolo, who wrote the piece with Cory Weinberg, said on X that Sora could be coming back in some form.

In the AI commentator Rohan Paul's summary, the third co-founder is Sujay Jaswa, a former Dropbox chief financial officer. The company aims to build AI video tools for filmmakers. Under terms said to be under discussion, it could heavily customise Sora and sell software built on it. Palazzolo says the buyers would be film studios.

OpenAI would receive an undisclosed equity stake in return, Paul wrote. The Information's article is paywalled and this paper has not read it in full, so these details come from the two posts. Neither OpenAI nor the startup has confirmed anything, and the startup has no public name or product.

Paul describes the model as shuttered, which is the point of the talks. A deal would give a product OpenAI has stopped selling a second life under outside control. Whether it would cover model weights or only API access is not stated in either post. No price or timeline has been reported.

stories.headline: Ambi raises $26M for an AI app that listens all day
stories.standfirst: Ambi, founded by a former Plaud executive, is releasing iPhone, Mac and Apple Watch apps that can record in the background, with ambient capture off by default.
body: Ambi has raised $26 million across several rounds for an app that listens in the background and offers suggestions in real time, TechCrunch reported. The company's co-founder and chief executive is Peter Mo, a former Plaud executive. Luminous Ventures, an early backer of Meituan and Unitree Robotics, led the rounds, and the device maker Huaqin also invested.

The apps work like a meeting note-taker, but users can choose to let them listen all day, according to the report. An AI agent draws on the user's calendar, meetings, knowledge base and web data to surface relevant information, and tasks can start on one device and continue on another. No price or release date was given.

Two more products are planned. An upcoming desktop app would observe users' work and store the important parts in memory to personalise suggestions, and a hardware device with a screen, speaker, camera and microphones is also on the way, again without a date. Ambi has more than 50 staff in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.

On privacy, TechCrunch said ambient capture is off by default and can be switched off at any time. Ambi says it does not store recordings and encrypts data, though it did not specify the method. The report notes it is unclear whether bystanders get enough warning, and Mo said users must tell others about ambient capture, calling disclosure an industry-wide problem.

stories.headline: Meta staff tease a model called Watermelon with fruit emoji
stories.standfirst: Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang posted watermelon emoji within minutes of each other on Monday, and TestingCatalog says Meta teased a model called Watermelon.
body: Meta's chief executive Mark Zuckerberg posted a photo on X on Monday with the caption "Muse ordered me 🍉 how thoughtful!", which had passed 2,400 likes when this paper read it. Thirteen minutes earlier, Alexandr Wang had posted "vibes kinda good 🍉", also without explanation. Neither post names a product.

TestingCatalog, which reports on unreleased AI features, said an upcoming model called "Watermelon" had been teased, and asked whether that meant training had finished. That is a guess, and the outlet's findings stay unconfirmed until the company ships. Meta has not announced a model, a date or a name.

The commentator kimmonismus wrote that Meta employees were hinting at a major release and that this week could be exciting. Another commentator, synthwavedd, said Watermelon is Meta's top-tier model, in the works for months and close to release, citing teasers from Meta staff. Both are bystanders relaying impressions rather than documents.

What the posts establish is narrow: two prominent Meta figures are using the same emoji on the same afternoon, which looks coordinated. What the model is, how large it is and whether it will have open weights are all unknown, and nothing here has been tested by anyone outside the company.

stories.headline: Microsoft says Maia 300 chip will carry most of its own AI inference
stories.standfirst: Satya Nadella says Microsoft will scale its Maia chips to multi-gigawatt deployments next year, and claims Maia 300 delivers 40 percent more tokens per watt than leading GPU-based systems.
body: Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella announced on X on Monday what he called the company's biggest bet yet on its own silicon. Starting next calendar year, he wrote, Microsoft will scale its Maia family of AI chips to multi-gigawatt deployments, making Maia the primary inference system for the company's own products and services.

Nadella introduced a new chip, Maia 300, and said it delivers 40 percent more tokens per watt than leading GPU-based systems. Microsoft has not published the benchmark behind that comparison in the post, and it does not say which GPU system it measured against. The figure is the company's own claim and has not been checked independently.

The post also described the current generation. Nadella said Microsoft is already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe and Australia, and that it delivers up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot, again by Microsoft's own measure.

Earlier press reports, citing The Information, said Microsoft was negotiating with TSMC for more than 300,000 Maia 300 units for 2027 delivery. A Microsoft Azure Maia manager was also quoted by Techzine as saying the chip was expected sometime in 2027. The announcement leaves unclear when Maia 300 reaches customers, and it gives no price or external customer list.

stories.headline: Users say Claude Opus 5.5 is being routed to a stronger unnamed model
stories.standfirst: TestingCatalog reports that X users saw Opus 5.5 requests land on a new, unnamed checkpoint over the weekend, with one demo reportedly using 27 million tokens to animate a scene in JavaScript.
body: Several X users reported over the weekend that requests to Claude Opus 5.5 appeared to be routed to a different, unannounced model, TestingCatalog reported on Monday. Users described outputs well above Opus 5.5's usual level. Anthropic has not confirmed any routing change, a new model or a name.

TestingCatalog cited a user called can, who said a one-sentence prompt with a Blender MCP connection produced a 3D model over about two hours without ready-made assets. Another user, Chetaslua, shared an animation drawn frame by frame in JavaScript from two prompts. The outlet reports it took about two hours and roughly 27 million tokens at maximum thinking effort.

Not every report was glowing. TestingCatalog said a user named Lumina found the difference from Opus 5.5 small, though the output looked slightly better. Kol Tregaskes suggested asking the model whether it knows VoxelBench without searching, but the outlet notes a yes would more likely show fresher training data than a smarter model.

On the name, TestingCatalog says speculation includes Opus 5.6 and Fable 5.5. It considers a new Opus test at least as likely as Fable, because traffic is being routed to Opus 5.5. The only official signal it cites is a post from Anthropic's John Hoffmann, who wrote that the best is yet to come and asked people to stay tuned.

Commentator kimmonismus separately wrote that a video of Anthropic's upcoming model showed it choosing images, music and visual direction and then coding the rest of the production in 2.5 hours, citing Chetaslua. The images and music were existing assets. All of this rests on user posts, and no benchmark or Anthropic statement has backed it.

stories.headline: DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus reaches Science with nine Erdős problems solved
stories.standfirst: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus, a Gemini-plus-Lean proof agent, solved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems, two unsolved for 56 years, in a peer-reviewed Science paper.
body: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus has been published in the journal Science, according to The Decoder, which reported on Monday that the system solved nine open Erdős problems, two of which had gone unsolved for 56 years. DeepMind attempted 353 of the problems, so the success rate is about 2.5 percent.

The system also proved 44 conjectures from the OEIS integer-sequence database, settled an open question in algebraic geometry and improved a known bound in min-max optimization, The Decoder says. An earlier Decoder report from May, on the preprint, put the OEIS attempt at 492 conjectures and described the algebraic-geometry question as 15 years old.

Per The Decoder, Nexus is built on Gemini 3.1 Pro, which drafts and revises proofs in the formal language Lean. Lean checks every draft after each edit, and its error messages steer the next attempt. For harder sub-problems the agent can call AlphaProof. DeepMind reports that it solved the nine Erdős problems even without AlphaProof, and the May report said a simpler variant could also manage all nine.

DeepMind has put the Lean proofs and prose versions in a public repository, google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results, under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY 4.0. The repository's README says anyone can verify the proofs by building the project with Lean's lake tool. At the time of writing it showed 312 stars. The README states it is not an official Google product.

The Decoder sets the paper against OpenAI, which posted hundreds of AI-written proofs on GitHub without journal review. The Decoder reports that the Association for Human Mathematics, which it says is led by Terence Tao, called for a boycott. The May report adds caveats: successes cluster where the Mathlib library is mature, and most Erdős problems stayed out of reach. We have not independently read the Science paper.

stories.headline: Microsoft's Brad Smith says a washing machine faces more safety rules than AI
stories.standfirst: Microsoft president Brad Smith told ITV that AI is less regulated than a carton of milk, and that the UK could lead on rules Washington has not written.
body: Microsoft president Brad Smith said in an ITV interview that AI is subject to fewer safety rules than everyday goods, Engadget reported on Monday. "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI," Smith said, adding that every carton of milk in a shop is subject to safety rules and inspection.

Smith argued that the lack of US action leaves the UK an opening to lead. According to Engadget, he said Washington does not view London as it views Brussels. He called that an advantage and said he hopes Microsoft and the UK government can take on the role.

On the most powerful models, those that could put global cybersecurity at risk, Smith said "the moment has arrived" for action. Engadget gives no detail of what rules he wants. We could not view the interview, so these remarks rest on that one report.

Engadget sets the remarks against a split in the industry. It says Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have reportedly voiced support for slowing development. President Trump has said the US industry should accelerate to stay ahead of China and favours self-regulation. Engadget also describes a summit pact, signed by industry leaders, that calls for self-regulation and independent auditors. Critics cited by the BBC call it a distraction.

stories.headline: Researchers teach a Unitree G1 humanoid to catch thrown boxes from camera alone
stories.standfirst: A University of Washington-led paper says its Reflex controller let a Unitree G1 catch human-thrown boxes 65 percent of the time at 2.5 metres, using only an onboard depth camera.
body: A team led by researchers at the University of Washington has published Reflex, a framework that teaches a humanoid robot to catch boxes thrown at it using only a camera on its own torso. The paper appeared on Hugging Face's daily papers on Monday with 55 upvotes. The authors, including Ranjay Krishna, list affiliations at Stanford, USC, the National University of Singapore and the Allen Institute for AI.

According to the paper, earlier systems often leaned on motion capture, marked objects or a hand-only controller. Reflex instead trains in three stages. A reinforcement-learning policy first learns whole-body motion from human references. A second stage compresses delayed, partial observations of the box into an eight-number description of its motion, with latency randomised between 20 and 60 milliseconds. A vision network then learns to predict that description from depth images.

On a real Unitree G1 with a torso-mounted RGB-D camera, the authors report catching human-thrown boxes 65 percent of the time at 2.5 metres, 40 percent at 5 metres and 15 percent at 7 metres, with 20 trials per distance. Three human catchers managed 85.0, 68.3 and 28.3 percent at the same ranges, so the robot reached 76 and 59 percent of human success at the first two distances, the paper says.

In simulation the visual controller caught 85.7 percent of throws, against 87.9 percent for a version given the box's true state. The authors also ran a 20-trial task chain in which success fell from 65 percent after the catch to 25 percent after carrying the box, handing it over and returning it. Their listed limits: one task, wide error bars of up to about 20 points, and a controller that is effectively blind to box size.
The paper links no code or project page, and no outside group has reproduced the results. All figures here are the authors' own, from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, so they may change.

stories.headline: Kling team says new diffusion training method cuts GPU hours 12-fold
stories.standfirst: KlingAI researchers say DiffusionART matched rival reinforcement-learning methods on a 13B video model with about 12 times fewer GPU hours, and removes the need to tune EMA.
body: Researchers from KlingAI have posted DiffusionART, a method for fine-tuning image and video generators with reinforcement learning from black-box rewards. The paper, dated Monday, drew 67 upvotes on Hugging Face's daily papers. It targets a trade-off. Reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO assign credit poorly and run slowly, the authors write. Forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are quick but unstable unless an exponential moving average is carefully tuned.

The authors argue the instability comes from a force in NFT-style objectives that pulls the forward and reverse processes apart. Positive and negative training only partly cancels it. DiffusionART instead pools each prompt's rewards into one shared improving direction. It adds a second, trust-region-masked update, which the paper claims removes the EMA tuning. It needs no differentiable reward model and could work with fewer samples per prompt, the authors suggest.

On text-to-video with HunyuanVideo-13B, the authors report reaching the late-stage mean reward of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 times fewer GPU hours, with mean training rewards 28.8 and 53.0 percent higher. On text-to-image with SD3.5-M, they say it reached Flow-GRPO's step-500 reward 10.0 times faster on GenEval, 5.2 on OCR and 9.6 on PickScore.

For image-to-video on Wan2.1-I2V-14B, the paper says a motion-quality score of 6 took 45.8 GPU hours against 220.3 for Flow-GRPO-Fast. A pairwise-feedback variant came close to scalar rewards, and, the authors say, using two samples rather than eight cut compute by 3.4 times on video, the authors say.

The page we read did not mention released code, and the numbers come from the authors' own experiments on a preprint. No independent group has reported reproducing them, so the claimed speedups may not hold elsewhere.

stories.headline: Palantir CTO says Pentagon already replaced Anthropic
stories.standfirst: Palantir's Shyam Sankar told CBS the Pentagon's drop of Anthropic had no operational impact because it "has already been replaced", and that AI makers own the liability for defective models.
body: Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar said the Pentagon's decision to stop using Anthropic products has had no operational impact, in an interview CBS News published on Sunday from Face the Nation. Asked about the move, he said the Defense Department "has a wide range of model providers" and that Anthropic's tools were "already replaced". Control over models, he argued, is institutions' "alpha", and none should depend on one provider.

On the Iran campaign, Sankar said "targeting is a process" and that AI does not pick targets: "That's not what's happening." He argued speed is the benefit. Executing many strikes in a day with one person working in hours, he said, "provides you a significant battlefield advantage", according to the CBS transcript.

Asked about the strike on a school in Minab that reportedly killed at least 123 children, Sankar said "we should wait for the final report". He rejected Bloomberg's reporting that personnel over-relied on AI, saying "The Bloomberg reporting is wrong", and attributed the cause to "human error". He said Palantir then built extra AI agents to double-check work. He offered no evidence for the cause in the interview.

On liability, Sankar said faulty AI is "a defective product" and that responsibility lies with "the AI companies of course". He used a car analogy: a defective car is the maker's problem, but driving it into a neighbour's house is the driver's. He added that existing law gives the field "a massive running head start".

These are Sankar's statements as published by CBS. Palantir is a Pentagon contractor, and neither the Defense Department nor Anthropic is quoted in the transcript. The paper has not independently confirmed the Minab findings or the replacement claim, which remain his account.

sources.author: CBS News: Face the Nation transcript with Shyam Sankar

stories.headline: Grok Bots can now be used by passengers in Tesla's Cybercab
stories.standfirst: X user Sawyer Merritt says he added laundry detergent to an Amazon cart by voice in a Cybercab, using a Grok Bot that signs out when he leaves.
body: Passengers can now use Grok Bots inside a Tesla Cybercab, according to a post on X by Sawyer Merritt that had about 800 likes when read on Monday morning. Merritt wrote that he tried it on a ride on Sunday night. The post includes a video of the feature.

Merritt says a rider signs into Grok once, after which their Bots are available on all future rides and are logged out automatically when they leave the vehicle, to protect privacy. He says the next ride signs the passenger back into apps they used before.

His test was adding laundry detergent to an Amazon cart by voice. He says the Bots can also send emails, place a coffee order and manage a calendar, finances or other tasks. These are Merritt's descriptions of what he tried or was told; Tesla has not published a feature list in anything seen for this story.

Elon Musk replied to the news on X with the words "Try Grok @Bot", which drew about 1,800 likes. Neither post says where the feature is live, which riders have it, or whether it is limited to a pilot group. No second rider has described it yet.

The claim rests on one rider's account and one clip. Tesla has not published a release note that the paper could find, and the privacy behaviour Merritt describes, the automatic sign-out at the end of a ride, has not been independently tested.

stories.headline: Amazon in talks to buy world-model startup Decart for about $7 billion
stories.standfirst: The Wall Street Journal reports Amazon is in talks to buy Decart for around $7 billion, after Anthropic reportedly walked away from a $6 billion deal.
body: Amazon is in talks to buy the AI startup Decart for around $7 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, according to a post relaying the report on X by the account Negligible Cap. The account added that Anthropic was said to have walked away from a $6 billion Decart acquisition. The reasons were not specified.

Negligible Cap speculated that Decart may have wanted more money. That is the account's guess, not reporting. The Journal's article itself was not available to this paper, so both figures rest on a secondhand summary.

Another X user, himanshustwts, says Anthropic cancelled during due diligence and describes Decart as a lab that builds world and video models. The same post says the company was valued at about $4 billion a quarter ago. That valuation was not confirmed by any source this paper opened.

Earlier reports, including one from Bloomberg in August, had Anthropic pursuing Decart at about $6 billion, and a later report said the deal was nearing signature at around $7 billion. Those reports named Nvidia as an existing investor. Neither Anthropic, Amazon nor Decart is quoted in anything seen for this story.

The reported turnaround is unconfirmed. Nothing seen here shows a signed agreement with Amazon, and the earlier accounts of an Anthropic deal conflict with the new one. Any of the parties could comment, and the terms could change.

stories.headline: US restores UK safety institute access to unreleased frontier AI models
stories.standfirst: The White House has reportedly reversed a decision that cut the UK's AI Security Institute off from unreleased models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
body: The White House has reinstated the UK's access to frontier AI models for safety testing after lobbying by British ministers, according to an exclusive posted on X by the journalist Tony Diver on Sunday. The US had earlier decided to restrict access to the latest models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Diver reports that the restriction was meant to stop the UK's AI Safety Institute from testing models before release. He says AI minister Kanishka Narayan was involved in the lobbying, and that ministers feared Britain's attempt to lead on AI regulation would otherwise be "dead in the water".

Another X user, Seb Johnson, says the change means the AI Security Institute can again reach the latest US models before launch and run its safety tests on them. That is his reading of Diver's report, not a separate confirmation.

No US or UK government statement was seen for this story, and the post does not say when the earlier restriction began or what conditions come with the restored access. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are not quoted.
The report rests on a single journalist's exclusive. The paper has not seen the linked article, and cannot say which agency made either decision or whether the access covers every lab.

stories.headline: Moonshot executives in talks to settle shareholder dispute before IPO
stories.standfirst: Reuters reports top executives at Kimi maker Moonshot AI are negotiating a settlement with a shareholder demanding compensation for alleged wrongdoing.
body: Top executives of the Chinese AI startup Moonshot are in talks to settle a legal dispute with a shareholder who is demanding compensation for their alleged wrongdoing, Reuters reported in an exclusive on Sunday. The talks come ahead of the company's planned Hong Kong listing.

Reuters posted the report on X in two items, one labelled "EXCLUSIVE" and citing "people" as its sources. The posts seen by this paper do not name the shareholder, the executives or the alleged wrongdoing, and give no settlement figure.
A headline from the news aggregator HuggingNews put the figure at $700 million. This paper could not confirm that number from Reuters' posts and does not rely on it.

Reuters reported in September that Moonshot had filed confidentially for a Hong Kong listing, aiming to raise about $3 billion. Moonshot has also faced US allegations about chips and distillation that it denies. Those earlier reports are background, and none of them mention the dispute.

Moonshot has not commented in anything seen for this story. Reuters' full article was not opened, so the details above are limited to what its posts say. No settlement has been announced, and talks may not conclude.

stories.headline: Veria says its AI agent found a 2015 XRP Ledger bug worth 18 trillion XRP
stories.standfirst: Veria Labs says its AI agent found and exploited a decade-old XRP Ledger overflow that could have created about 18 trillion XRP in one transaction. Ripple paid the top $250,000 bounty.
body: Veria Labs, an AI security startup, says its AI agent found a critical flaw in the XRP Ledger's payment engine. The bug could have let an attacker create about 18 trillion XRP in one transaction, The Block reported on Sunday. Co-founder Cayden Liao told the outlet the agent also built a working exploit.

RippleX, the ledger's developer, shipped a fix in xrpld version 3.4.1 on 25 September, three days after Veria reported the bug. The disclosure report states there is "no evidence that this issue was exploited on any public network," The Block reported. Liao said Ripple paid the top bounty of $250,000, which he called the largest ever paid for a bug found entirely by an AI agent.

The flaw dates to 2015 and chains two bugs, The Block said. The payment engine summed the cost of many order-book offers filled at once with no overflow check, so a large enough total wrapped around to a small number. A related check on newly created XRP had its own addition issue, so it would not have stopped the minting. Liao said each bug alone would be low severity.

An attacker would have needed a few hundred accounts listing tiny token fractions for large amounts of XRP, then one payment closing all the sales, per the report. The sellers would be paid in full while the buyer paid a few hundred drops plus the fee. Liao put the potential creation at roughly 184 times the 100 billion XRP cap. Those figures are Veria's scenario, not a loss.

The patch skipped the usual amendment vote, which needs more than 80 percent of trusted validators over two weeks, The Block reported, calling that a first in more than ten years of amendments. More than 80 percent of validators on the default list ran the fix that day. The 3.4.1 source code followed about two weeks after the binaries, which drew criticism from Cyber Capital founder Justin Bons.

RippleX engineer Mayukha Vadari said "You can't sneak a critical bug patch into a routine public release process." Head of engineering J. Ayo Akinyele said "AI is fundamentally changing how quickly vulnerabilities can be discovered," and that RippleX will expand AI-assisted bug hunting. We could not open the disclosure report itself, and Veria's claims about the exploit have not been independently verified.

stories.headline: Coinbase's Armstrong says a fine-tuned 9B open model beat frontier models at fraud checks
stories.standfirst: Coinbase's Brian Armstrong says a Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuned on internal data beat frontier models at payments fraud checks, faster and cheaper. No figures were published.
body: Brian Armstrong, Coinbase's chief executive, posted on X on Sunday that the company fine-tuned an open-weights model, Qwen3.5-9B, on proprietary internal data. He said it "out performed frontier models, at much lower cost and speed" on one specialised task, fraud prevention. The post had more than 3,000 likes when we read it.

The post gives no benchmark, no error rates and no names for the frontier models it was compared against. Coinbase has not published a technical write-up that we could find, so the claim rests on Armstrong's account alone. The post carries two images, which we could not examine in detail, and no one outside Coinbase has tested the model.

Armstrong frames it as a pattern he expects to spread. "The frontier models are amazing generalists," he wrote, but specialist models will increasingly beat them on narrow tasks. He also suggested some backend services at Coinbase could be replaced entirely by this architecture, without saying which ones.

The company is building the tooling to make that routine, he said. Coinbase has an internal skill in its employee agent harness that takes a request such as "/fine-tune-and-serve-llm I want to fine-tune Qwen for payments risk review" and starts the training. Armstrong did not say how many teams use it or what it costs to run.

stories.headline: Karpathy puts people who have watched frontier agents work at about 20 million
stories.standfirst: Andrej Karpathy's napkin maths: 6 billion people have barely touched an LLM, 20 million have watched agents finish months of coding from a prompt, and about 5,000 have frontier systems internally.
body: Andrej Karpathy reposted an April thought on X on Sunday, saying the gap in shared understanding of what language models can do is "widening" and is now "a sharp funnel". By the time we read it the post had about 22,500 likes and more than two million views, and the Hacker News front page carried it with 253 points.

His napkin maths has four tiers. Around 6 billion people, about 75 percent of the population, have barely met an LLM. Another 1 to 2 billion are casual users of free-tier chatbots and see, in his words, "derpy chatbots". He gives these as estimates, not measurements, and says some professionals outside maths and code sit in this tier too. He presents all of this as his own estimate.

Then come roughly 20 million people, 0.2 percent, who use frontier models for maths and code and see "first-hand" that projects that took weeks or months can be completed by agents from a prompt. Karpathy lists building, copying and translating apps. He says that less than a year ago he was still typing code by hand.

At the top, he says, are about 5,000 people with internal access to frontier systems. Karpathy describes the external preview as swarms of thousands of agents working for weeks on software projects, finding zero-day flaws and advancing mathematics, while human review falls behind. These are his characterisations, and he gives no sources for the head counts.

He offers three drivers: impact scales with the size of the problem, capability peaks where tasks are digital and verifiable, because of reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards, and access varies across free, paid and internal tiers. The result, he writes, is the "weirdness of the moment", with a small group feeling "the vertigo of the curve going vertical".

stories.headline: Hugging Face's Delangue says OpenAI's maths proofs are now open training environments
stories.standfirst: A community dataset turns 369 Lean 4 results OpenAI published this month into tasks where an agent writes the proof. Clément Delangue calls it rough: an equivalent proof can still score zero.
body: Clément Delangue, Hugging Face's chief executive, posted on Sunday that his team had turned OpenAI's maths problems into open-source reinforcement-learning environments on the platform. He called the work "early and rough" and said it shows research releases becoming "executable training infrastructure for everyone". The post had about 940 likes when we read it.

The dataset, FineEnvs/openai-math, holds 369 Lean 4 theorem-proving tasks for the Harbor framework, according to its page. They are ported from OpenAI's openai/math release, which formalises 405 results; the dataset keeps the 369 whose official proofs were verified end to end. It is licensed Apache-2.0, with the statements credited to OpenAI.

In each task an agent gets a sandbox with Lean 4 and Mathlib, no internet access and a theorem whose proof is replaced by `sorry`. A separate sandbox then checks the answer. The page says it scores 1 only if the statement matches the original exactly, uses only standard axioms and passes the Lean kernel, and 0 otherwise.

That strictness is the caveat Delangue flagged: an equivalent reformulation, or partial progress, also scores zero. The page adds that the problems are open research questions so near-zero rewards are expected, and that the statements and proofs have been public since 6 October, which makes contamination possible. Thirty-six statements were excluded after failing validation.

Running it is not light. Each task asks for 4 CPUs, 8 GB of memory and 10 GB of disk and gives the agent four hours, according to the page, and the sandbox image takes about an hour to build. The authors call it experimental. We found no training results reported from it yet.

stories.headline: Apple tested an Apple TV with built-in Siri microphones, Bloomberg's Gurman reports
stories.standfirst: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports Apple tested an Apple TV 4K that hears Siri directly, and a remote with a speaker, ahead of an event expected on Tuesday.
body: Apple has tested built-in microphones and a refreshed Siri Remote for an upgraded Apple TV 4K, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in his Power On newsletter on Sunday, as summarised by 9to5Mac. Apple has not announced either feature, and Gurman describes them as tested, not confirmed products.

The microphones would let people "shout Siri commands at the set-top box", in Gurman's words, instead of using the remote or a paired HomePod, as today. The refreshed remote would add a speaker, which Gurman says would make it "easier to find between couch cushions". Today's remote has only a basic Find feature.

9to5Mac says Apple's "Welcome home" event is set for Tuesday 13 October, where it expects the new Apple TV 4K. Gurman expects the Apple TV and a new HomePod mini to be available from 30 October, according to the same summary, with the HomeView smart display following in mid-November.

TechCrunch, also relying on Gurman, describes HomeView as a Siri-powered device with a display and an A18 chip that controls other smart-home gear, reportedly in countertop and wall-mounted versions. It says earlier reporting pointed to an LG partnership for a smart lock, thermostat and doorbell. No prices have been reported.

Both outlets draw on one Bloomberg source, so this is a single line of reporting, not two independent confirmations. The Siri features here are about voice input, and neither report describes any new AI model behind them. Apple has announced nothing, and none of it is official until the event.
